scenes.title: A factory, for software
scenes.define: A written route that every piece of work follows. Agents do each stop the same way every time, scripts check the result, and people approve at the gates.
scenes.explain: A software factory is a written route that every piece of work follows. Agents do each stop the same way every time, scripts check the result, and people approve at the gates. It is the difference between asking an assistant to write some code and running a process you can trust, repeat, and inspect.

scenes.title: Six words to know
points: The stops a piece of work passes through, in order.
One job. Done by an agent, or by a script.
How a stop is done, written down once.
Where the work waits for a person to approve.
Proof that a stop passed its checks.
Picks up new work and keeps it moving.
scenes.explain: Six words describe the whole thing. A route is the list of stops work passes through. A stop is one job, done by an agent or a script. A skill is how a stop is done, written down once. A gate is where the work waits for a person. Evidence is the proof a stop passed. The background job picks up new work and keeps it moving.

scenes.title: Build one in two minutes
scenes.say: Each repository gets its own factory. Here is one being created from scratch: a fast lane for bug reports.
scenes.explain: Each repository gets its own factory, made in the editor. These frames are the real thing being created: a fast lane for bug reports on the API repository. Name it, point it at the repository, pick a starting point, say which label triggers it, and switch it on.
scenes.how:
python3 factory/editor.py
Click Add a repository. Every field you see in these frames is on that page.

scenes.say: Open the editor and add a repository
Give the factory a name and point it at the code
Pick a starting point. These are examples to edit, not fixed types.
The factory exists. This is its route.
Say what triggers it: a label, and who the issue is assigned to
Arrange the stops. A gate is where a person must approve.
Write the team's rules, and the commands that prove a change works
Switch it on and save. From here it runs by itself.

scenes.title: Nobody starts it
scenes.say: A job on the machine checks for new work every ten minutes. No one types a command.
scenes.explain: Once a factory is switched on, a background job checks its tracker every ten minutes. Nobody types a command. Here a bug was filed on GitHub with the label and the assignee the factory watches for. The next pass picked it up, and within three minutes agents had reproduced the bug with a failing test, fixed it, run the tests and reviewed the fix.

scenes.say: The Activity page: the factory is running, with nobody at the keyboard
A person files a bug. The label and the assignee are what the factory looks for.
The next pass finds it and puts an agent to work
Its own log: picked up, reproduced, fixed, reviewed, then it stops

scenes.title: The gate holds
scenes.say: The factory stops and waits. A person reads what was done, and decides.
scenes.explain: At a gate the factory stops, however long it takes. The Activity page shows what is waiting and the documents the agents wrote, so the person approving can read exactly what they are agreeing to. One click approves. The background job then finishes the route and opens a pull request. Merging is still a person's decision.
scenes.how:
Open the Activity tab. Or from a terminal:
python3 factory/flow.py --target factory-demo-api-bugs approve GH4

scenes.say: Waiting for you: the route has stopped at its gate
First, read what the agents did
Then a person approves. This click is the human decision.
The route finishes on its own and opens a pull request
The pull request on GitHub, waiting for a person to merge

scenes.title: Features take more stops
scenes.say: The same factory, a different route: requirements, design, tasks, build, proof.
scenes.explain: A bug needs a short route. A feature needs a longer one, and the factory is the same. On the API repository, design is required and there are two gates before any code, because API changes are costly to undo. On the UI repository the gate is at the end, where a person looks at the screens. A route is whatever your work needs.
scenes.how: In the editor, use the arrows to reorder stops, Add a gate, or Add a stop.

scenes.say: The API route has two gates before any code is written
The UI route puts its second gate at the end
An agent wrote requirements with exact inputs and exact responses
Both routes stop at their gate until a person approves

scenes.title: Done means proven
scenes.say: Every task names a skill. One agent builds, another checks, and a script checks the checker.
scenes.explain: The work is split into small tasks and every task names the skill that builds it; a script rejects a task list where one does not. A maker agent builds each task. A separate checker runs the gate and writes an evidence sheet of what was expected against what was found. Then the factory's own script re-runs those checks and the tests. Work ticked without evidence is sent back automatically.
scenes.how: The lint-tasks, check-evidence and verify stops are scripts. They cost nothing and cannot be talked round.

scenes.say: Every task names the skill that builds it
The evidence sheet: expected against found, check by check
The factory re-runs the checks itself before moving on
The task board before
And after: what the UI route built from one issue
It ends in a pull request, with the proof attached

scenes.title: No process, no review
scenes.say: Every pull request is checked by a script first. Only work that followed the process earns an agent's time.
scenes.explain: A review route checks pull requests, whoever wrote them. A script goes first: is there a spec, does every task name a skill, is there evidence, did the tests change with the code, plus the team's own rules. A quick hack added by hand, with no spec and no test, was stopped by the script and cost nothing. The request the factory built passed all 11 checks, and only then did an agent review the code.
scenes.how: Label a pull request factory-review. Set the rules in the Review rules tab.

scenes.say: A quick hack with no spec and no test: stopped by the script
The request the factory built passes all 11 checks
Only then does an agent review the code
You decide how strict each check is
And you add your own rules by filling in a sentence

scenes.title: Three issues in, three pull requests out
scenes.say: 5 gates approved by a person. Everything else was done by agents and checked by scripts. Agent cost for the whole run: $10.69.
scenes.explain: Three issues became three open pull requests across two repositories, each backed by a spec or a reproduction, evidence, and passing tests. A person approved five gates and will decide what to merge.
